title: More members, less money
units_note: All money figures in ₹ lakh unless marked. Bookings are cash sales in the month, excluding GST.

brief.headline: Record sign-ups. Bookings down 24%.
brief.story: FitKaro is a home-workout app with live classes and diet plans, sold as a ₹399 monthly or ₹2,999 annual subscription. September brought more paying members than any month before, and the app's ratings held up. But cash bookings fell by almost a quarter. The founders are about to raise a seed round and need to explain the dip.

body.text: Refunds were ₹0.6L in August and ₹0.7L in September. GST is excluded and the rate didn't change.
FIT70 was created on 20 Aug for one influencer campaign. It has no usage limit and no expiry date.

evidence.teaser: Where visitors to the sign-up page came from

body.text: desideals.in is a coupon and deals aggregator.
“Got a whole year for ₹900 with FIT70, crazy deal.”
Rival app Pulse launched a ₹1,999 annual plan on 5 September, backed by a TV campaign.
FitKaro trainers' fees rose ₹1L in September for two new class formats.

causes.label: Members are cancelling faster
causes.feedback: Monthly churn was flat at about 7%, and early annual cancellations barely moved.

causes.label: A competitor's cheaper plan took the full-price buyers
causes.feedback: New members went up. The full-price buyers didn't leave; most of them paid ₹900 with FIT70 instead.

causes.label: An influencer's 70%-off code leaked to a deals site, and full-price buyers used it
Prices were cut
causes.feedback: The list prices haven't changed since January.

causes.label: Ad spend became inefficient
causes.feedback: Ad spend rose only ₹0.5L and traffic grew. The problem is what people paid, not how many came.

causes.label: App bugs drove people away
causes.feedback: Ratings held at 4.5 and member numbers grew.

causes.label: The WELCOME10 offer got expensive
causes.feedback: WELCOME10 uses actually fell, and it's only 10% off one month.

causes.label: Trainer fees went up
causes.feedback: That's a cost of ₹1L. It doesn't change bookings.

causes.label: Fewer people visited the sign-up page
causes.feedback: Visits went up, mostly from one new source.

causes.label: A GST rate change
causes.feedback: Bookings exclude GST, and the rate didn't change.

causes.label: Influencer marketing is too expensive
causes.feedback: Influencer fees were flat at ₹2L. The influencer isn't the problem; an uncapped code is.

bonus.question: What should the founders do first?
options: Cancel every subscription bought with FIT70
Cap or expire FIT70 now, honour the people who already bought, and give each influencer a unique, limited code
Cut the annual price to ₹1,999 to match Pulse
bonus.explanation: Every day FIT70 stays open, full-price buyers keep paying ₹900. Closing it stops the leak today. Cancelling existing buyers' subscriptions would turn a pricing mistake into a trust problem, and a ₹1,999 price cut gives away revenue that isn't being lost to Pulse.

explanation.answer: FIT70, a 70%-off annual code made for one influencer, had no limit or expiry. It reached desideals.in in early September, and 1,900 people paid ₹900 for a ₹2,999 plan. Full-price annual sales fell from 1,960 to 600, so about 1,400 people who would have paid ₹2,999 paid ₹900. That's roughly ₹42L lost against ₹17L collected: ₹25L, the whole drop.
fastest_path: Open the bookings statement. Full-price annual sales collapsed from ₹58.8L to ₹18.0L while a coupon line jumped to ₹17.1L.
Open the coupon report. FIT70 went from 40 uses to 1,900, with no cap or expiry.
Open traffic sources. 14,800 visits came from a coupon site that didn't exist in August.
traps: Pulse's ₹1,999 plan launched the same month and is the easy story for investors. But new members rose.
Record sign-ups make it look like growth. The members are real; the price they paid wasn't.
"Influencer marketing is too expensive" is close, but the fee was flat. The leak was the code's settings.
explanation.lesson: Every discount code is a price list someone else can publish.
